label: thexpcokerintro
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thexpcokerintro}
Let $X$ be a smooth variety of dimension $d$ over~$\mathbb{R}$. Let~$\mathcal{L}$ be a line bundle on $X$. For $0\leq c\leq d$ and $0\leq n\leq d$, the cokernel of the higher signature morphism $\operatorname{sign}_{n,X}^c:\mathrm{H}^c(X,\mathbf{I}^n(\mathcal{L}))\to \mathrm{H}^c(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z}(\mathcal{L}))$ is killed by~$2^{d-n}$.
head: environment

label: thexpcokeroptimalintro
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thexpcokeroptimalintro}
Fix $0\leq c\leq d$ and $0\leq n< d$. There exists a smooth variety $X$ of dimension~$d$ over~$\mathbb{R}$ such that the cokernel of 
$$\operatorname{sign}_{n,X}^c:\mathrm{H}^c(X,\mathbf{I}^n)\to \mathrm{H}^c(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})$$ 
is not killed by~$2^{d-n-1}$. If $d-c\leq 4$, one can moreover choose $X$ to be projective.

title: Theorem

Let $X$ be a smooth cubic hypersurface of dimension $d$ over $\mathbb{R}$ with $X(\mathbb{R})$ disconnected. 
If $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, or if~$d=4$ and~$X$ is very general, then the cokernel of the signature morphism $\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{nr}}(X)\to \mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})$ is not killed by $2^{d-1}$. If~$d\geq 5$, this cokernel is killed by~$2^{d-1}$.

title: Proposition

\label{prop:weak_lefschetz}
Fix $c,d\geq 0$. Let $Y$ be a smooth projective variety over $\mathbb{R}$, of dimension $c+d$. Let $\mathcal{E}$ be an ample vector bundle of rank $c$ on $Y$. Let $\tau\in \mathrm{H}^0(Y,\mathcal{E})$ be such that the zero locus $X\subset Y$ of $\tau$ is smooth of codimension $c$. Let $M$ be a~$G$\nobreakdash-module. Then the restriction homomorphism 
$$\mathrm{H}_G^j(Y(\mathbb{C}),M)\to\mathrm{H}_G^j(X(\mathbb{C}),M)$$
is an isomorphism for $j<d$ and is injective if $j=d$.

label: propva
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{propva}
Let $X$ be an abelian variety of dimension $d\geq 1$ over $\mathbb{R}$ such that~$X(\mathbb{R})$ has $2^d$ connected components. Then $\operatorname{\overline{ev}}^{d-1}_X$ is not surjective.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The $G$-module $\Lambda:=\mathrm{H}_1(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})$ is isomorphic to $(\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}(1))^{\oplus a}\oplus \mathbb{Z}[G]^{\oplus (d-a)}$ for some $a\geq 0$, and $X(\mathbb{C})$ is $G$-equivariantly diffeomorphic to $(\Lambda\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{R})/\Lambda$ 
                           
(see e.g.\,\cite[\S\S4--5]{silholRealAbelianVarieties1982}). It follows that  the $G$-equivariant diffeomorphism class of $X(\mathbb{C})$ only depends on the number of connected components of $X(\mathbb{R})$, so we may assume that $X=E^d$ for some elliptic curve $E$ over $\mathbb{R}$ such that~$E(\mathbb{R})$ has $2$ connected components. Let $(p_i:X\to E)_{1\leq i\leq d}$ be the projections.

Applying Theorem \ref{thm:image_of_total_restriction_to_the_real_locus} to $E$ (noting that $w_E=1$ because the tangent bundle of~$E$ is trivial) shows the existence of $\alpha\in \mathrm{H}^1_G(E(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}/2)$ with $r_E^1(\alpha)=(0,[E(\mathbb{R})])$, where~$[E(\mathbb{R})]\in \mathrm{H}^1(E(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z}/2)$ is the fundamental class of $E(\mathbb{R})$. Define
$$\beta:=p_1^*\alpha\smile\dots\smile p_d^*\alpha\quad\text{in }\mathrm{H}^d_G(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}/2).$$
It follows from \cite[(1.28)]{benoistIntegralHodgeConjecture2020} that $r^d_X(\beta)=(0,\dots, 0,[X(\mathbb{R})])$. We deduce from Theorem \ref{thm:image_of_total_restriction_to_the_real_locus} applied to $X$ (noting that $w_X=1$ because the tangent bundle of~$X$ is trivial) that for all $\gamma\in \mathrm{H}^{d-1}_G(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}/2)$, one has ${\deg(r_X^{d-1}(\gamma)\smile r_X^d(\beta))=0}$. This exactly means that the number of connected components of $X(\mathbb{R})$ on which~$\operatorname{\overline{ev}}_X^{d-1}(\gamma)$ is nonzero is even, which proves the proposition.
head: environment

label: thtriangle
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{thtriangle}
Let $X$ be a smooth variety over $\mathbb{R}$. Let $M\xrightarrow{a} N\xrightarrow{b} P\xrightarrow{c}$ be a distinguished triangle in the bounded derived category of $G$-modules and fix $j\in\mathbb{Z}$.  
The image of the composition
$$\mathrm{H}^{j-1}_{\mathrm{nr}}(X,P)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}^{j-1}_{\mathrm{nr},X,P}}\mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathrm{H}^{j-1}(G,P))\xrightarrow{c_*} \mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathrm{H}^j(G,M))$$
contains the image by $\operatorname{ev}^j_{X,M}$ of $\{\alpha\in \mathrm{H}^j_G(X(\mathbb{C}),M)\mid a_*\alpha\textrm{ has coniveau }\geq 2\}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\alpha\in\mathrm{H}^j_G(X(\mathbb{C}),M)$ be a class such that $a_*\alpha$ has coniveau $\geq 2$. Let~${Z\subset X}$ be a closed subset of codimension $\geq 2$, with complement $U:=X\setminus Z$, such that~$(a_*\alpha)|_{U}=0$ in~$\mathrm{H}^j_G(U(\mathbb{C}),N)$. The long exact sequence associated with the triangle yields the existence of $\beta\in \mathrm{H}^{j-1}_G(U(\mathbb{C}),P)$ such that $c_*\beta=\alpha|_{U}$.

Bloch--Ogus theory identifies the unramified cohomology group $\mathrm{H}^{j-1}_{\mathrm{nr}}(X,P)$ with the subgroup of $\operatorname{colim}_V \mathrm{H}^{j-1}_G(V(\mathbb{C}),P)$ (where $V$ runs over all dense open subsets of $X$) consisting of those classes whose residues along all codimension $1$ integral subvarieties of $X$ vanish (see \cite[(5.1) and (5.2)]{benoistIntegralHodgeConjecture2020}, and note that the arguments given there apply to bounded complexes of $G$-modules as well as to $G$-modules). 

As $Z$ has codimension $\geq 2$, it follows that $\beta$ induces an unramified cohomology class $\gamma\in \mathrm{H}^{j-1}_{\mathrm{nr}}(X,P)$. By construction, the class $c_*\gamma\in \mathrm{H}^j_{\mathrm{nr}}(X,M)$ is the unramified cohomology class associated with $\alpha$. It follows that $c_*\operatorname{ev}^{j-1}_{\mathrm{nr},X,P}(\gamma)=\operatorname{ev}^j_{X,M}(\alpha)$.

label: cortriangle1
title: Theorem

title: Proof
body_md:
In each of the four cases, we apply Lemma \ref{thtriangle} with $j=d$ and $M=\mathbb{Z}/2$ to an appropriate distinguished triangle $\mathbb{Z}/2\xrightarrow{a} N\xrightarrow{b} P\xrightarrow{c}$\,. In all cases, the induced morphism $\mathrm{H}^{d-1}(G,P)\xrightarrow{c_*} \mathrm{H}^d(G,\mathbb{Z}/2)=\mathbb{Z}/2$ is bijective. One therefore deduces from the conclusion of Lemma \ref{thtriangle} and from the surjectivity of $\operatorname{\overline{ev}}^d_X$ (see Theorem \ref{thKvH}) that~$\operatorname{ev}_{\mathrm{nr},X,P}^{d-1}$ is surjective. In each case, this is equivalent to the desired assertion.

The short exact sequence of $G$-modules $0\to\mathbb{Z}[G]\to\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}(1)\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to 0$ induces a distinguished triangle $\mathbb{Z}/2\to\mathbb{Z}[G][1]\to(\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}(1))[1]\to$\,. Applying Lemma \ref{thtriangle} to it yields \ref{cori}.

To prove \ref{corii}, apply Lemma~\ref{thtriangle} to the distinguished triangle stemming from the short exact sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to\mathbb{Z}/2[G]\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to 0$.

Assertion \ref{coriii} is obtained by applying Lemma \ref{thtriangle} to the distinguished triangle $\mathbb{Z}/2\to K_d\to L_d\to$ appearing in \eqref{diagtriangle}. That the conclusion of Lemma \ref{thtriangle} implies the desired result in this case follows from Lemma \ref{lemLd}.

Finally, to prove \ref{coriv}, apply Lemma \ref{thtriangle} to the distinguished triangle \eqref{triangleJ}.
head: environment

label: cortriangle2
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
All assertions follow from the respective assertions of Theorem~\ref{cortriangle1}. 

To show that the hypothesis of Corollary~\ref{cortriangle2}\,\ref{coroi} implies that of Theorem~\ref{cortriangle1}\,\ref{cori}, use the short exact sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}[G]\to\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}(1)\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to 0$.

Case \ref{coroii} is immediate.

Suppose that the assumptions of \ref{coroiii} are satisfied. Taking the $G$-equivariant cohomology of the second row of \eqref{diagtriangle} yields an exact sequence
\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{H}^d(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})\to\mathrm{H}^d_G(X(\mathbb{C}),K_d)\to\mathrm{H}^{d+1}(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}).
\end{equation*}
As $\mathrm{H}^{d+1}(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})[2]=0$, any $2$-torsion class in $\mathrm{H}^d_G(X(\mathbb{C}),K_d)$ lifts to $\mathrm{H}^d(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})$, and hence has coniveau $\geq 2$. Applying Theorem \ref{cortriangle1}\,\ref{coriii} proves \ref{coroiii}.

Assume finally that the hypotheses of \ref{coroiv} hold. Taking $G$-equivariant cohomology in \eqref{dist1}, we get an exact sequence
$$\mathrm{H}^{d-1}(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}/2)\to\mathrm{H}^d_G(X(\mathbb{C}),J)\to\mathrm{H}^{d}(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}/2).$$
As $\mathrm{H}^{d}(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}/2)=0$ and $\mathrm{H}^{d-1}(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}/2)$ has coniveau $\geq 2$, we deduce that all classes in~$\mathrm{H}^d_G(X(\mathbb{C}),J)$ have coniveau $\geq 2$ and one can apply Theorem \ref{cortriangle1}\,\ref{coriv}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Some other particular cases of Lemma \ref{thtriangle} are of interest. For instance, applying it to the distinguished triangle associated with the short exact sequence 
$0\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}[G]\to(\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}(1))\to 0$
 shows that if $\mathrm{H}^d(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})[2]$ has coniveau $\geq 2$, then the evaluation map $\mathrm{H}^{d-1}_{\mathrm{nr}}(X,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}(d))\to \mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z}/2)$ is surjective.
The study of evaluation maps with $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}(j)$ coefficients parallels that with $\mathbb{Z}/2$ or~$\mathbb{Z}(j)$ coefficients, but we do not pursue it for lack of specific motivation.

title: Proof
body_md:
We verify the hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{th3bis}\,\ref{th3bisi}. In doing so, we identify the canonically isomorphic $G$-modules $\mathbb{Z}(2)$ and $\mathbb{Z}(4)$. Let $\pi:X_{\mathbb{C}}\to X$ be the base change morphism. Fix $\alpha\in\mathrm{H}^4_G(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}(2))$ of coniveau $\geq2$, hence algebraic. Assume that $\alpha=2\beta$ for some $\beta\in\mathrm{H}^4_G(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}(2))$. Since $\pi^*\alpha$ is algebraic, it is Hodge, and hence so is $\pi^*\beta$. By hypothesis, there exists $\beta'\in\ker(\operatorname{ev}_X^4)$ with~${\pi^*\beta'=\pi^*\beta}$.
Applying $\pi_*$ to this identity shows that $2\beta'=2\beta$, hence that~$\alpha=2\beta'$.

label: propciquadrics
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{propciquadrics}
Let $X$ be a smooth complete intersection of two quadrics of dimension $d$ over~$\mathbb{R}$ such that $X(\mathbb{R})$ is not connected. If $d\in \{1,2,3\}$, then $\operatorname{\overline{ev}}^{d-1}_{\mathrm{nr},X}$ is not surjective. If~$d\geq 4$, then $\operatorname{ev}^{d-1}_{\mathrm{nr},X}$ is surjective.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $d\in \{1,2,3\}$. In view of Corollary \ref{corpetitdegre}, it suffices to show that $\operatorname{\overline{ev}}^{d-1}_{X}$ is not surjective, which is a consequence of Proposition \ref{prop:image_global_sign_hypersurface}.

When $d\geq 4$, we verify the two hypotheses of Corollary \ref{cortriangle2}\,\ref{coroiii}. First, one has~$\mathrm{H}^{d+1}(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})[2]=0$ by the weak Lefschetz theorem and Poincar\'e duality. Second, the cohomology group $\mathrm{H}^d(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})$ has coniveau $\frac{d}{2}\geq 2$ if $d$ is even by \cite[Corollary 3.15]{reidCompleteIntersectionQuadrics1972} and coniveau $\frac{d-1}{2}\geq 2$ if $d$ is odd by \cite[Theorem~4.14\,(b) p.\,73]{reidCompleteIntersectionQuadrics1972}. In more detail, when $d$ is odd, Reid constructs a smooth projective curve $C$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and an isomorphism~$\mathrm{H}^1(C(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})\ext@arrow 0359\arrowfill@\relbar\relbar{\setbox\z@\hbox{$\rightarrow$}\dimen0\ht\z@\multiply\dimen0 6\divide\dimen0 10\ht\z@\dimen0\box\z@}{}{\,\sim\,} \mathrm{H}^{d}(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})$ (called \emph{cylinder homomorphism}) induced by an algebraic correspondence. Since this correspondence is given by a cycle of dimension $\frac{d+1}{2}$, the image of this isomorphism has coniveau~$\frac{d-1}{2}\geq 2$.
head: environment

label: propcubic
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For  $d\in \{1,2,3\}$, combine Proposition \ref{prop:image_global_sign_hypersurface} and Corollary \ref{corpetitdegre}.

Suppose that $d=4$ and that $X$ is very general. By Proposition~\ref{prop:image_global_sign_hypersurface}, the morphism~$\operatorname{\overline{ev}}^3_{X}$ is not surjective. To conclude the proof in this case, it therefore suffices to verify the hypothesis of Corollary \ref{corth3bis}. Let $\pi:X_{\mathbb{C}}\to X$ be the base change morphism, let $h\in \mathrm{H}^2_G(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}(1))$ be the hyperplane class in $G$\nobreakdash-equivariant cohomology, and identify $\mathbb{Z}(2)$ and $\mathbb{Z}(4)$. Let $\alpha\in \mathrm{H}^4(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})$ be a Hodge class. Since~$X$ is very general, all Hodge classes in $\mathrm{H}^4(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})$ are multiples of $(\pi^*h)^2$ by \cite[Chap.\,1, Proof of Corollary 2.12]{huybrechtsGeometryCubicHypersurfaces2023} and primitivity of $(\pi^*h)^2$ in $\mathrm{H}^4(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})$. It follows that $\alpha=\ell (\pi^*h)^2=\pi^*(\ell h^2)$ for some $\ell\in\mathbb{Z}$. This concludes because, the class $h^2$ being algebraic, one has $\operatorname{ev}^4_X(h^2)=0$.

For $d\geq 5$, apply Corollary \ref{cortriangle2}\,\ref{coroiii}, whose hypotheses are satisfied by the weak Lefschetz theorem and Poincar\'e duality, and by Lemma \ref{lemconiveaucubic} below.

label: lemconiveaucubic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemconiveaucubic}
Let $X$ be a smooth cubic hypersurface of dimension $d\geq 1$ over $\mathbb{C}$. Then $\mathrm{H}^d(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})$ has coniveau $\geq \lfloor\sqrt{6d+37}-6\rfloor$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume first that $X$ is general. Set $k:= \lfloor\sqrt{6d+37}-6\rfloor$. This is the largest integer $k$ satisfying 
\cite[(2.3)]{lewisCylinderHomomorphisms1993} (note that in \cite{lewisCylinderHomomorphisms1993}, the integers $n$ and $d$ denote the dimension and the degree of $X$). We apply the results of \cite{lewisCylinderHomomorphisms1993} with this value of $k$ (this is legitimate as indicated in the note added in proof in \cite[p.\,220]{lewisCylinderHomomorphisms1993}).

Lewis constructs a smooth projective variety $\Omega_X$ of dimension $d-2k$ over~$\mathbb{C}$ and a cylinder homomorphism $\Phi_*:\mathrm{H}^{d-2k}(\Omega_X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})\to \mathrm{H}^d(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})$ induced by an algebraic correspondence, so the image of $\Phi_*$ has coniveau $\geq k$ (see~\mbox{\cite[(3.7)]{lewisCylinderHomomorphisms1993}}). The lemma follows since $\mathrm{H}^d(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})$ is equal to $\operatorname{im}(\Phi_*)$ if $d$ is odd, and is generated by $\operatorname{im}(\Phi_*)$ and a power of the hyperplane class if $d$ is even (see \cite[p.\,213]{lewisCylinderHomomorphisms1993}).

The result for arbitrary $X$ follows from the case of a general $X$ by a specialization argument (exactly as in the second part of \cite[Proof of Proposition 10]{fu2CyclesHypersurfacesCubiques2019}).
head: environment

label: propva2
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{propva2}
Let $X$ be an abelian variety of dimension $d$ over $\mathbb{R}$ such that~$X(\mathbb{R})$ has $2^d$ connected components. If $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, or if $d=4$ and $X$ is principally polarized and very general, then $\operatorname{\overline{ev}}^{d-1}_{\mathrm{nr},X}$ is not surjective.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition \ref{propva}, the morphism $\operatorname{\overline{ev}}^{d-1}_{X}$ is not surjective. To conclude, we show that the images of $\operatorname{\overline{ev}}^{d-1}_{X}$ and $\operatorname{\overline{ev}}^{d-1}_{\mathrm{nr},X}$ coincide. When~${d\in\{1,2,3\}}$, this follows from Corollary \ref{corpetitdegre}. Assuming from now on that $d=4$ and that~$X$ is principally polarized and very general, it remains to verify the hypothesis of Corollary~\ref{corth3bis}.

Let $\pi:X_{\mathbb{C}}\to X$ be the base change morphism, let $\theta\in \mathrm{H}^2_G(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}(1))$ be the class of the principal polarization in $G$\nobreakdash-equivariant cohomology, and identify $\mathbb{Z}(2)$ and~$\mathbb{Z}(4)$. Fix a Hodge class $\alpha\in \mathrm{H}^4(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})$. As the abelian variety~$X$ is principally polarized and very general, Mattuck's theorem (see \cite[Theorem~17.4.1]{birkenhakeLangeComplexAbelianVarieties2004}) and the fact that~$\frac{(\pi^*\theta)^2}{2}\in\mathrm{H}^4(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})$ is primitive imply that $\alpha=\ell\frac{(\pi^*\theta)^2}{2}$ for some $\ell\in\mathbb{Z}$. By Lemma \ref{lemvapp} below applied with $d=4$ and $c=2$, there exists~$\eta\in\ker(\operatorname{ev}^4_X)$ such that $\pi^*\eta=\frac{(\pi^*\theta)^2}{2}$. It follows that $\alpha=\pi^*(\ell\eta)$, which concludes the proof.
head: environment

label: lemvapp
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemvapp}
Let $X$ be a principally polarized abelian variety of dimension~$d$ over~$\mathbb{R}$ such that $X(\mathbb{R})$ has $2^d$ connected components. Let $\theta\in \mathrm{H}^2_G(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}(1))$ be the class of the principal polarization. Fix $1\leq c\leq d$. There exists $\eta\in\mathrm{H}^{2c}_G(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}(c))$ vanishing in restriction to each real point of $X$ such that the image of $\theta^c-c!\,\eta$ in~$\mathrm{H}^{2c}(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})$~vanishes.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $E$ be an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{R}$ such that $E(\mathbb{R})$ has $2$ connected components. By the connectedness of the parameter space for principally polarized abelian varieties $X$ of dimension $d$ over $\mathbb{R}$ such that $X(\mathbb{R})$ has $2^d$ connected components (see \cite[Proposition 9.3]{grossHarrisRealAlgebraicCurves1981} or \cite[IV, Definition 4.4, Corollary 4.5, Theorem 4.6]{silholRealAlgebraicSurfaces1989}), and since the statement is purely topological, we may assume that $X=E^d$ and that the principal polarization is induced by principal polarizations of the factors.

Let $Z\subset X$ be the union of the $\binom{d}{d-c}$ abelian subvarieties of $X=E^d$ that are products of~$d-c$ of the factors. Let $\eta\in\mathrm{H}^{2c}_G(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}(c))$ be the image of $Z$ by the $G$\nobreakdash-equivariant cycle class map (for which see \cite{krasnovEquivariantGrothendieckCohomology1994} or \cite[\S 1.6.1]{benoistIntegralHodgeConjecture2020}). The class~$\eta$ vanishes upon restriction to the real points of $X$ because it is algebraic, and the assertion concerning its image in $\mathrm{H}^{2c}(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z})$ is a direct computation.

label: thm:functorial_Krasnov
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:functorial_Krasnov}
Let $X$ be a smooth algebraic variety of dimension $d$ over $\mathbb{R}$. The homomorphism of sheaves $\overline{\operatorname{ev}}_\mathrm{nr}^d:\mathscr{H}_X^d(\mathbb{Z}/2)\to\iota_*\mathbb{Z}/2$  has a canonical section.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $U$ is an open subset of $X$ and $V$ is a connected component of $U(\mathbb{R})$, we let $\overline{\sigma}_V\in\mathrm{H}_G^d(U(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}/2)$ be the equivariant fundamental class of $V$ \cite[p. 15]{benoistIntegralHodgeConjecture2020}. For fixed $U\subseteq X$, the assignment $V\mapsto\overline{\sigma}_V$ extends to a group morphism 
\[\overline{\sigma}(U):\mathrm{H}^0(U(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z}/2)\to\mathrm{H}_G^d(U(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}/2).\] 
 By \cite[Remark 1.6 (ii)]{benoistIntegralHodgeConjecture2020}, one has $\overline{\operatorname{ev}}_U^d\circ\overline{\sigma}(U)=\operatorname{Id}$. The definition of the equivariant fundamental class shows that the morphisms $\overline{\sigma}(U)$ are natural in~$U$, hence determine a morphism $\overline{\sigma}$ of presheaves from $\iota_*\mathbb{Z}/2$ to the presheaf~${U\mapsto\mathrm{H}_G^d(U(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}/2)}$. Let~$\overline{\sigma}_\mathrm{nr}:\iota_*\mathbb{Z}/2\to\mathscr{H}_X^d(\mathbb{Z}/2)$ be the sheafification of~$\overline{\sigma}$. As sheafification is a functor, the equality $\overline{\operatorname{ev}}^d\circ\overline{\sigma}=\operatorname{Id}$ of endomorphisms of $\iota_*\mathbb{Z}/2$ implies that $\overline{\operatorname{ev}}_\mathrm{nr}^d\circ\overline{\sigma}_\mathrm{nr}=\operatorname{Id}$. The morphism $\overline{\sigma}_\mathrm{nr}$ is then the required section.

label: cor:mod_2_cycle_class_map_surjective
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:mod_2_cycle_class_map_surjective}
Let~$X$ be a smooth algebraic variety of dimension~$d$ over $\mathbb{R}$. For all~${c\geq 0}$, the morphism $\mathrm{H}^c(X,\mathscr{H}_X^d(\mathbb{Z}/2))\to\mathrm{H}^c(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z}/2)$ obtained from~${\overline{\operatorname{ev}}_\mathrm{nr}^d}$ by taking cohomology in degree $c$ admits a canonical section.

title: Proof
body_md: This follows from the fact that ${\overline{\operatorname{ev}}_\mathrm{nr}^d}$ has a canonical section (see Theorem~\ref{thm:functorial_Krasnov}), by functoriality of cohomology.

label: propmultiplicative
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{propmultiplicative}
Fix $d\geq 0$ and $0\leq n<d$. Set $X:=\mathbb{G}_{m,\mathbb{R}}^d$. The cokernel of the signature morphism $\operatorname{sign}_{n,X}^0:\mathrm{H}^0(X,\mathbf{I}^n)\to\mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})$ is not killed by $2^{d-n-1}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $(t_1,\ldots,t_d)$ be the coordinates of $X$. If $I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_l\}$ is a subset of~$\{1,\ldots,d\}$, we consider the quadratic form \[q_{I,n}:=\varepsilon_{|I|,n}\otimes\langle 1,-t_{i_1}\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes\langle 1,-t_{i_l}\rangle\in\mathrm{H}^0(X,\mathbf{I}^n),\] where, given an integer $0\leq l\leq d$, the form $\varepsilon_{l,n}$ is defined as
\[\varepsilon_{l,n}:=\left\{\begin{array}{cl}
\langle 1,1\rangle^{\otimes n-l} & \text{if}\;l\leq n\\
\langle 1\rangle                 & \text{if}\;l>n.
\end{array}\right.\]

Applying the proof of \cite[Lemma 2.16]{bachmannMilnorWittMotives2025} to $\mathbf{I}$-cohomology instead of $\mathbf{K}^{\text{MW}}$\nobreakdash-cohomology (making use of homotopy invariance \cite[Théorème 11.2.9]{faselGroupesChowWitt2008} and purity \cite[Theorem 2.41]{hornbostelRealCycleClass2021} for $\mathbf{I}$-cohomology) shows that
$$\mathrm{H}^0(\mathbb{G}_{m,\mathbb{R}}^d,\mathbf{I}^n)=\mathrm{H}^0(\mathbb{G}_{m,\mathbb{R}}^{d-1},\mathbf{I}^n)\oplus \mathrm{H}^0(\mathbb{G}_{m,\mathbb{R}}^{d-1},\mathbf{I}^{n-1})\cdot\langle 1,-t_d\rangle,$$
with the convention that $\mathbf{I}^m=\mathbf{W}$ when $m\leq 0$. Induction on $d$ then implies that~$\mathrm{H}^0(X,\mathbf{I}^n)$ is the free abelian group generated by the forms $(q_{I,n})_{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}$.

Given an open and closed subset $A$ of $X(\mathbb{R})$, we let $\chi_A\in\mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})$ denote its characteristic function. The set $\pi_0(X(\mathbb{R}))$ of connected components of $X(\mathbb{R})$ is in bijection with the set of subsets $I$ of $\{1,\ldots,d\}$ via the association $I\mapsto A_I$, where
\[A_I:=\{(t_i)_i\in X(\mathbb{R})\mid t_i<0\;\text{if}\;i\in I\text{ and }t_i>0\;\text{if}\;i\notin I\}.\] 
We conclude that $(\chi_{A_I})_{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}$ is a basis of $\mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}^{\pi_0(X(\mathbb{R}))}$. Set further 
$$B_I:=\{(t_i)_i\in X(\mathbb{R})\mid t_i<0\;\text{if}\;i\in I\}.$$
Then $A_{I}=B_I\setminus\bigcup_{i\notin I}B_{I\cup\{i\}}$. For $\{i_1,\dots, i_k\}=J\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\}\setminus I$, one computes that~$B_{I\cup\{i_1\}}\cap\cdots\cap B_{I\cup\{i_k\}}=B_{I\cup\{i_1,\ldots,i_k\}}$, so the inclusion-exclusion formula yields 
\[\chi_{A_I}=\sum_{k=0}^{d-|I|}(-1)^{k}\sum_{J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\setminus I,\,|J|=k}\chi_{B_{I\cup J}}.\] 
We deduce that the family $(\chi_{B_I})_{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}$ generates $\mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})$. Since its cardinality is the rank $2^d$ of this free abelian group, it follows that $(\chi_{B_I})_{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}$ is in fact a basis of $\mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})$. 

For $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, set $u_{I,n}:=\max(2^{|I|-n},1)\in\mathbb{Z}$. By definition, one has \[\operatorname{sign}_{n,X}^0(q_{I,n})=u_{I,n}\chi_{B_I}.\] We conclude that $\operatorname{sign}_{n,X}^0:\mathrm{H}^0(X,\mathbf{I}^n)\to\mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})$ is an isomorphism onto the subgroup of $\mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})$ generated by the $(u_{I,n}\chi_{B_I})_{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}$, hence that the cokernel of $\operatorname{sign}_{n,X}^0$ is isomorphic to $\bigoplus_{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}\mathbb{Z}/u_{I,n}$. This group is not killed by~$2^{d-n-1}$ because $u_{\{1,\ldots,d\},n}=2^{d-n}$.

label: prop:cokernel_cubic
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:cokernel_cubic}
Let $X\subseteq\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ be a smooth cubic hypersurface of dimension~$d\leq 4$. If $d=4$, we further assume that~$X$ is very general. Fix $0\leq n\leq d$. The image of 
$$\operatorname{sign}_{n,X}^0:\mathrm{H}^0(X,\mathbf{I}^n)\to\mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})$$
is generated by $1\in \mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})$ and by the multiples of $2^{d-n}$.

If $n<d$ and $X(\mathbb{R})$ is disconnected, the cokernel of $\operatorname{sign}_{n,X}^0$ is not killed by~$2^{d-n-1}$.
head: environment

label: signsignev
title: Proof
body_md:
The second assertion is a direct consequence of the first, which we now prove.

We argue by decreasing induction on $n$. When $n=d$, the morphism $\operatorname{sign}_{n,X}^0$ is surjective by \cite[Corollary 5.2]{lerbetImageHigherSignature2026}, which proves the proposition in this case. Suppose from now on that $n<d$. We will rely on the commutative exact~diagram
\begin{equation}
\label{signsignev}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=small, column sep=small]
	0 & {\mathrm{H}^0(X,\mathbf{I}^{n+1})} & {\mathrm{H}^0(X,\mathbf{I}^n)} & {\mathrm{H}^0(X,\mathscr{H}_X^n(\mathbb{Z}/2))=\mathrm{H}_\mathrm{nr}^n(X,\mathbb{Z}/2)} \\
	0 & {\mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})} & {\mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})} & {\mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z}/2)}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{\operatorname{sign}_{n+1,X}^0}"', from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=1-4]
	\arrow["{\operatorname{sign}_{n,X}^0}"', from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow["{\overline{\operatorname{ev}}_{\mathrm{nr},X}^n}"', from=1-4, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\cdot 2}"', from=2-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=2-4]
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
obtained by taking cohomology in (\ref{eq:milnor_conjecture}).

Assume first that $d=4$ (so $X$ is very general) and $n=3$. It follows from the proof of Proposition \ref{propcubic} for $d=4$ (see how Proposition~\ref{prop:image_global_sign_hypersurface} and Corollary~\ref{corth3bis} are combined there) that the image of $\overline{\operatorname{ev}}_{\mathrm{nr},X}^3$ is generated by~$1\in\mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z}/2)$. We deduce from \eqref{signsignev} that the image of $\operatorname{sign}_{3,X}^0$ is contained in the subgroup generated by~$1\in \mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})$ and by the multiples of $2$. The class $1\in \mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})$ is in the image of $\operatorname{sign}_{3,X}^0$ because $\operatorname{sign}_{3,X}^0(\langle 1,1\rangle^{\otimes 3})=1$. So are the multiples of~$2$ by \eqref{signsignev} and the surjectivity of $\operatorname{sign}_{4,X}^0$ (the base case of the induction). This completes the proof of the proposition in this case.

We henceforth assume that $n\leq 2$. Restriction and sheafification morphisms fit into a commutative square
\begin{equation}
\label{restrictionsheafification}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=small, column sep=small]
	{\mathrm{H}_G^n(\mathbb{P}^{d+1}(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}/2)} & {\mathrm{H}_G^n(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Z}/2)} \\
	{\mathrm{H}_\mathrm{nr}^n(\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{R}^{d+1},\mathbb{Z}/2)} & {\mathrm{H}_\mathrm{nr}^n(X,\mathbb{Z}/2)}
	\arrow["\sim", from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[two heads, from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
of abelian groups, whose top horizontal arrow is bijective by Proposition~\ref{prop:weak_lefschetz} (as~${n<d}$) and whose right vertical arrow is surjective by Lemma \ref{lemmepetitdegre} (as~$n\leq 2$).
It follows from~\eqref{restrictionsheafification} that the morphism $\mathrm{H}_\mathrm{nr}^n(\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{R}^{d+1},\mathbb{Z}/2)\to\mathrm{H}_\mathrm{nr}^n(X,\mathbb{Z}/2)$ is surjective. The morphism~$\mathrm{H}^n_{\mathrm{nr}}(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z}/2)\to\mathrm{H}^n_\mathrm{nr}(\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{R}^{d+1},\mathbb{Z}/2)$ given by pullback from the point is surjective (see \cite[Proposition 1.2]{colliot-theleneVarietesUnirationnellesNon1989}, and use the comparison between \'etale and $G$\nobreakdash-equivariant cohomology \cite{coxEtaleHomotopyType1979}), hence so is~${\mathrm{H}^n_{\mathrm{nr}}(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z}/2)\to\mathrm{H}_\mathrm{nr}^n(X,\mathbb{Z}/2)}$. The class $\langle 1,1\rangle^{\otimes n}\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,\mathbf{I}^n)$ is sent by the top right horizontal arrow of \eqref{signsignev} to the image in~$\mathrm{H}_\mathrm{nr}^n(X,\mathbb{Z}/2)$ of the nonzero element of~$\mathrm{H}^n_{\mathrm{nr}}(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z}/2)$, hence to a generator of~$\mathrm{H}_\mathrm{nr}^n(X,\mathbb{Z}/2)$. We deduce from \eqref{signsignev} that $\mathrm{H}^0(X,\mathbf{I}^n)$ is generated by~$\mathrm{H}^0(X,\mathbf{I}^{n+1})$ and $\langle 1,1\rangle^{\otimes n}$. As~$\operatorname{sign}_{n,X}^0(\langle 1,1\rangle^{\otimes n})=1$, it follows from \eqref{signsignev} again that the image of $\operatorname{sign}_{n,X}^0$ is generated by~$1\in \mathrm{H}^0(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})$ and by twice the image of~$\operatorname{sign}_{n+1,X}^0$. The induction hypothesis completes the proof.

label: propPfistercubic
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $d\geq 5$, one can use \cite[Proposition 1]{debarreSurIntersectionsCompletes2000} to find a $2$-dimensional linear subspace~$\Pi\subset X$. Let $\widetilde{\mathbb{P}^{d+1}_{\mathbb{R}}}\to \mathbb{P}^{d+1}_{\mathbb{R}}$ and $\widetilde{X}\to X$ be the blowups along $\Pi$, so $\widetilde{X}$ is the strict transform of $X$ in $\widetilde{\mathbb{P}^{d+1}_{\mathbb{R}}}$. Let $\pi':\widetilde{\mathbb{P}^{d+1}_{\mathbb{R}}}\to\mathbb{P}^{d-2}_{\mathbb{R}}$ and $\pi:\widetilde{X}\to\mathbb{P}^{d-2}_{\mathbb{R}}$ be the projections from $\Pi$. As $\pi'$ is a $\mathbb{P}^3$-bundle and $\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{\mathbb{P}^{d+1}_{\mathbb{R}}}}(\widetilde{X})$ has degree~$2$ on the fibers of $\pi'$, each fiber of $\pi$ is isomorphic to a $\mathbb{P}^3$, or to a possibly singular quadric surface.

By birational invariance of $\mathrm{H}^0(X,\mathbf{I}^{d-1})$, it suffices to show that 
$$\operatorname{sign}^0_{d-1,\widetilde{X}}:\mathrm{H}^0(\widetilde{X},\mathbf{I}^{d-1})\to\mathrm{H}^0(\widetilde{X}(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})$$
is surjective. Fix a connected component $K\subset \widetilde{X}(\mathbb{R})$. By definition of~$\operatorname{sign}^0_{d-1,\widetilde{X}}$, we must find ${q_K\in \mathrm{H}^0(\widetilde{X},\mathbf{I}^{d-1})}$ whose signature, when viewed as an element of~$\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{nr}}(\widetilde{X})$, is equal to $2^{d-1}$ on $K$ and to $0$ on the other connected components of~$\widetilde{X}(\mathbb{R})$. 

We first construct $q_K$. The above description of the fibers of $\pi$ implies that the real loci of the real fibers of $\pi$ are empty or connected. The compact subsets~$\pi(K)$ and~${\pi(\widetilde{X}(\mathbb{R})\setminus K)}$ of~$\mathbb{P}^{d-2}(\mathbb{R})$ are therefore disjoint. Applying the Stone--Weierstrass theorem to an affine open neighborhood~$U\subset\mathbb{P}^{d-2}_{\mathbb{R}}$ of~$\mathbb{P}^{d-2}(\mathbb{R})$ yields a rational function~${f}$ on~$\mathbb{P}^{d-2}_{\mathbb{R}}$ that is regular along~$\mathbb{P}^{d-2}(\mathbb{R})$, negative on~$\pi(K)$, and positive on~${\pi(\widetilde{X}(\mathbb{R})\setminus K)}$. Define~$q_K$ to be the Pfister form $\langle 1,-f\rangle\otimes\langle 1,1\rangle^{\otimes d-2}$. The form~$q_K$ belongs to $\mathrm{I}^{d-1}(\mathbb{R}(\widetilde{X}))$ and has the required signature by our choice of~$f$. It remains to prove that~$q_K$ belongs to the subgroup~${\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{nr}}(\widetilde{X})}$.
 
Fix an integral divisor $D\subset \widetilde{X}$. Set~$F:=\mathbb{R}(D)$. Our goal is to show that the residue of~$q_K$ along~$D$ vanishes. If the order of vanishing $\operatorname{ord}_D(f)$ of $f\in\mathbb{R}(\widetilde{X})$ along~$D$ is even, this is automatic (see e.g.\,\cite[Remark 19.12]{elmanKarpenkoMerkurjevQuadraticForms2008}). We may therefore assume that~$\operatorname{ord}_D(f)$ is odd. Then the residue is a multiple of~$\langle 1,1\rangle^{\otimes d-2}$ (again by \cite[Remark 19.12]{elmanKarpenkoMerkurjevQuadraticForms2008}). We will show that this form vanishes in~$\mathrm{W}(F)$. 

Set $D':=\pi(D)$ and $F':=\mathbb{R}(D')$. As $\operatorname{ord}_D(f)$ is nonzero, the inclusion ${D'\subset \mathbb{P}^{d-2}_{\mathbb{R}}}$ is strict, so we have $\dim(D')\leq d-3$. It follows from \cite[Theorem~31.22 and Corollary~35.29]{elmanKarpenkoMerkurjevQuadraticForms2008} that any class in~$\mathrm{I}^{d-2}(F')$ whose signatures with respect to all field orderings of $F'$ vanish must be the trivial class. If $F'$ admits no field ordering, this implies that $\mathrm{I}^{d-2}(F')=0$, hence that $\langle 1,1\rangle^{\otimes d-2}$ already vanishes in $\mathrm{W}(F')$. We henceforth assume that $F'$ admits at least one field ordering.

Let $Q$ be the generic fiber of $\pi|_D:D\to D'$. It is an irreducible component of a fiber of $\pi$, so either it is a smooth quadric surface or one has $Q(F')\neq\varnothing$. We claim that~$Q$ has no point in any real closed extension of $F'$. As $F'$ admits a field ordering, it follows that $Q$ must be a smooth quadric surface. To prove the claim, note that~$f$ is invertible along~$\widetilde{X}(\mathbb{R})$, so $D(\mathbb{R})=\varnothing$. We deduce from the Tarski--Seidenberg transfer principle (see \cite[Proposition 5.2.3]{BochnakCosteRoy1998}) that~$D$ has no point in any real closed extension of $\mathbb{R}$. Hence $Q$ has no point in any real closed extension of~$F'$.
 
 Let $a,b,c\in (F')^\times$ be such that the form $\langle 1,a,b,c\rangle$ is an equation of $Q$. Since~$Q$ has no point in any real closed extension of $F'$, the elements~$a,b,c$ are positive with respect to all the field orderings of $F'$. The forms~$\langle1,a\rangle\otimes\langle1,b\rangle\otimes\langle1,c\rangle\otimes\langle1,1\rangle^{\otimes d-5}$ and~$\langle1,1\rangle^{\otimes d-2}$ therefore have identical signatures. Since both belong to $\mathrm{I}^{d-2}(F')$, they are equal in $\mathrm{W}(F')$. As the Pfister form $\langle1,a\rangle\otimes\langle1,b\rangle\otimes\langle1,c\rangle$ contains~$\langle 1,a,b,c\rangle$ as a subform, it is isotropic over $F'(Q)=F$, hence hyperbolic over $F$ (see \cite[Corollary 9.10]{elmanKarpenkoMerkurjevQuadraticForms2008}). Thus $\langle1,1\rangle^{\otimes d-2}$ vanishes in $\mathrm{W}(F)$, as required.

label: lem:P1_suspension_image_quadratic_real_cycle_class_map
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:P1_suspension_image_quadratic_real_cycle_class_map}
Let $c,d,n\geq 0$ be integers. Let $X$ be a smooth variety of dimension~$d$ over $\mathbb{R}$ and let $\mathcal{L}$ be a line bundle on $X$. Let $p:\mathbb{P}_X^1\to X$ be the structural morphism. Then $\operatorname{sign}_{n,X}^{c}$ is a retract of~$\operatorname{sign}_{n+1,\mathbb{P}_X^1}^{c+1}$, in the sense that there exists a diagram
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{\mathrm{H}^{c}(X,\mathbf{I}^{n}(\mathcal{L}))} & {\mathrm{H}^{c+1}(\mathbb{P}_X^1,\mathbf{I}^{n+1}(p^*\mathcal{L}))} \\
	{\mathrm{H}^{c}(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z}(\mathcal{L}))} & {\mathrm{H}^{c+1}(\mathbb{P}_X^1(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z}(p^*\mathcal{L}))}
	\arrow["\alpha"', shift right=2, from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{\operatorname{sign}_{n,X}^{c}}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["\beta"', from=1-2, to=1-1]
	\arrow["{\operatorname{sign}_{n+1,\mathbb{P}_X^1}^{c+1}}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\alpha'}", shift left=2, from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\beta'}", from=2-2, to=2-1]
\end{tikzcd}\]
whose inner and outer squares commute and such that ${\beta\circ\alpha=\operatorname{Id}}$ and $\beta'\circ\alpha'=\operatorname{Id}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
If $c=d$, take $X:=(\mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{R}})^c$. As $\operatorname{sign}_{c,X}^c$ is surjective by Corollary~\ref{cor:integral_cycle_class_map_split_surjective}, diagram~\eqref{signsignnc} implies that the cokernel of $\operatorname{sign}_{n,X}^c$ is not killed by $2^{d-n-1}$.

Assume now that $c<d$. To prove the first assertion, apply Proposition \ref{propdeYaX} to~$Y:=\mathbb{G}_{m,\mathbb{R}}^{d-c}$ (this is legitimate by Proposition \ref{propmultiplicative}). To prove the second assertion, apply it to a very general smooth projective cubic hypersurface $Y$ of dimension~${d-c}$ over~$\mathbb{R}$ such that $Y(\mathbb{R})$ is disconnected (use Proposition \ref{prop:cokernel_cubic}).

title: Corollary
body_md: Let $X$ be a smooth variety of dimension $d$ over $\mathbb{R}$. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be a line bundle on $X$. For all $0\leq c\leq d$, the cokernel of the real cycle class map~${\widetilde{\operatorname{cl}}_{\mathbb{R}}:\widetilde{\mathrm{CH}}^c(X,\mathcal{L})\to \mathrm{H}^c(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z}(\mathcal{L}))}$ is killed by~$2^{d-c}$.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md: Fix $0\leq c<d$. There exists a smooth variety~$X$ of dimension $d$ over $\mathbb{R}$ such that the cokernel of the real cycle class map~${\widetilde{\operatorname{cl}}_{\mathbb{R}}:\widetilde{\mathrm{CH}}^c(X)\to \mathrm{H}^c(X(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{Z})}$ is not killed by~$2^{d-c-1}$. If $d-c\leq 4$, one can moreover choose $X$ to be projective.
